title: Who runs out first?
hook: There are fewer O₂ molecules. So O₂ runs out first?

knows: that a chemical equation is a recipe of molecule counts
that molecules are counted in whole numbers
doesNotKnow: that the recipe's ratio, not the smaller pile, decides which reactant limits

misconception: The reactant you have fewer of limits the reaction.
objective: The learner can explain that with 6 H₂ and 4 O₂, the 2:1 recipe uses up the H₂ after 3 O₂, making 6 H₂O and leaving 1 O₂, so the limiting reactant is found by matching at the ratio.

claims.text: Hydrogen and oxygen react as 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
claims.source: Standard balanced equation (Brown et al., Chemistry: The Central Science, ch. 3).

claims.text: From 6 H₂ and 4 O₂ the most H₂O you can make is 6, with 1 O₂ left over.
claims.source: Sets of (2 H₂ + 1 O₂): min(floor(6/2), 4) = 3 sets → 6 H₂O; O₂ left = 4 − 3 = 1; H₂ left = 0. Node script; Demo.tsx computes MOST = min(H0, 2·O0).

claims.text: 6 H₂ need only 3 O₂, so the H₂ runs out first even though there is more of it.

recall.question: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. You have 2 N₂ and 9 H₂. Which runs out first?
recall.why: 2 N₂ need 6 H₂ and 9 are on hand, so the N₂ runs out first. Match the piles at the 1:3 ratio; the smaller pile is not what decides.
